questions.skill: One-to-one functions
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why does a strictly increasing function have an inverse function?
questions.prompt_markup: Why does a strictly increasing function have an inverse function?

choices.text: Its graph passes through the origin, so it can be reflected over y = x.
Different inputs give different outputs, so each output comes from exactly one input.
Its outputs are always positive, so each output can be undone.
Its domain is all real numbers, so every input has an output.

questions.correct_answer: Different inputs give different outputs, so each output comes from exactly one input.
questions.grading_note: Strictly increasing implies one-to-one. The others name properties (passing through the origin, positive outputs, domain) that do not make a function one-to-one.

questions.skill: Restrict the domain to make a function invertible
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: f(x) = (x - 3)² is not invertible on all real numbers. Which restriction and inverse are correct?
questions.prompt_markup: f(x) = (x - 3)² is not invertible on all real numbers. Which restriction and inverse are correct?
questions.grading_note: On x ≥ 3, y = (x - 3)² gives x = 3 + √y. On x ≤ 3 the inverse is 3 - √x; x ≥ 0 is not one-to-one (f(2) = f(4)).

questions.prompt: h(x) = x² has h(-2) = 4, h(0) = 0, and h(2) = 4. Why is h⁻¹(4) not defined, and how can the domain be restricted to fix it?
questions.prompt_markup: h(x) = x² has h(-2) = 4, h(0) = 0, and h(2) = 4. Why is h⁻¹(4) not defined, and how can the domain be restricted to fix it?

choices.text: 4 is the output of two inputs (-2 and 2); restrict h to x ≥ 0 (or to x ≤ 0).
0 has no inverse, so remove x = 0 from the domain of h.
4 is the output of two inputs (-2 and 2); restrict h to -2 ≤ x ≤ 2.
h⁻¹(4) = 1/4, so it is defined, and no restriction is needed.

questions.correct_answer: 4 is the output of two inputs (-2 and 2); restrict h to x ≥ 0 (or to x ≤ 0).
questions.grading_note: Each half of the parabola is one-to-one; -2 ≤ x ≤ 2 still contains both inputs.

questions.prompt: f(x) = (x - 3)² has range y ≥ 0. When its domain is restricted to make it invertible, why should the restricted function still take every output value y ≥ 0?
questions.prompt_markup: f(x) = (x - 3)² has range y ≥ 0. When its domain is restricted to make it invertible, why should the restricted function still take every output value y ≥ 0?

choices.text: So the restricted function has more outputs than the original function, which makes the inverse larger.
So the inverse is defined for every output of the original function; for example, x ≥ 3 still gives every y ≥ 0.
Because the inverse function must be identical to the original function on the restricted domain.
Because a restricted function must always have exactly the same domain as the original function.

questions.correct_answer: So the inverse is defined for every output of the original function; for example, x ≥ 3 still gives every y ≥ 0.
questions.grading_note: Keeping the original range keeps the inverse defined on all of it.
